title: THE UNTOLD STORY BEHIND BENAIAH KILLING TWO LION-LIKE WARRIORS OF MOAB
paragraphs: THE UNTOLD STORY BEHIND BENAIAH KILLING TWO LION-LIKE WARRIORS OF MOAB
Some stories in Scripture flash across the page so quickly that most readers never stop to realize they are standing on holy ground.
And then the story is gone.
Overshadowed by kings, prophets, giants, and battles.
Benaiah is one of those names.
Yet hidden inside a brief passage is one of the most astonishing displays of courage, faithfulness, and spiritual symbolism in the entire Old Testament.
“Benaiah son of Jehoiada was a valiant fighter from Kabzeel, who performed great exploits. He struck down Moab’s two mightiest warriors…” (2 Samuel 23:20, NIV)
Most English translations render the phrase differently.
This is why many translations render the phrase as:
The kind of men entire armies feared.
The kind of men whose reputations traveled ahead of them.
The kind of men who became legends while still alive.
The text gives no dramatic battle scene.
As though heaven assumes courage needs no embellishment.
He struck down two of Moab's greatest champions.
But if we pause and imagine the reality, the weight becomes staggering.
Moab was not some insignificant nation.
The Moabites had a long and complicated relationship with Israel.
These lion-like warriors represented everything that intimidated ordinary men.
The answer may not be found in his muscles.
It may be found in his heart.
The Bible repeatedly introduces him as:
His father was a priestly figure.
Benaiah grew up where faith mattered.
He learned that victories are not determined merely by swords but by the God who holds nations in His hands.
“You come to me with sword and spear and javelin, but I come to you in the name of the LORD of hosts.” (1 Samuel 17:45)
Benaiah belonged to the same spiritual lineage of courage.
Not courage because danger was absent.
And isn't that where most of us struggle?
We all have our own lion-like warriors.
The memory of what happened years ago.
The wound that still bleeds when nobody is looking.
Those giants seem larger than us.
We start negotiating with what God called us to conquer.
But Benaiah's story reminds us that intimidating does not mean invincible.
The enemy often wins before the battle ever begins because fear convinces us defeat is certain.
Yet Scripture repeatedly reveals a different reality.
The God who raised the dead.
The God revealed fully in Jesus Christ.
But Benaiah's story becomes even more extraordinary.
“He also went down into a pit on a snowy day and killed a lion.”
Most people use snow as an excuse.
Benaiah treated it as a battlefield.
Everything about this scene feels irrational.
Faith often looks reckless to people who do not understand trust in God.
There is a difference between foolishness and faith.
Throughout Scripture, God's servants repeatedly stepped into situations others considered impossible.
Peter stepped out of the boat.
And Jesus walked toward the cross.
The Kingdom of God has always advanced through people willing to trust beyond what appears reasonable.
Yet his greatest achievement may not have been killing warriors.
It may have been remaining faithful when nobody was watching.
Years later, Benaiah would become one of David's most trusted men.
Eventually he would serve under Solomon and rise to one of the highest positions in the kingdom.
His public promotion was built upon private faithfulness.
God often tests character before assigning influence.
Perhaps that is why Benaiah's story resonates so deeply today.
They are fighting battles nobody applauds.
Remaining faithful in seasons nobody celebrates.
But heaven sees every act of obedience.
Nothing escapes the attention of God.
And this brings us to the greater story.
Because every hero in Scripture ultimately points beyond himself.
Benaiah's courage points toward a greater Warrior.
His victory points toward a greater Deliverer.
His faith points toward a greater Savior.
The Greek New Testament reveals Him.
When the angel announced His birth, he declared:
The name Jesus comes from the Hebrew:
And that is exactly what He came to do.
But conquer the deepest enemies of humanity.
The greatest lion humanity ever faced was not roaming a pit.
It was the power of sin that held every human heart captive.
Yet Christ stepped into that pit willingly.
And through His death and resurrection He achieved the victory none of us could accomplish ourselves.
This is why the Gospel remains the greatest story ever told.
Not because good people become better.
Not because the broken are discarded.
Not because scandal has the final word.
That truth sits at the heart of everything we do.
Maybe you see yourself in Moab's warriors.
Maybe you see yourself in the lion pit.
Or maybe you see yourself in Benaiah.
Still believing God has not finished writing your story.
The same God who strengthened Benaiah still transforms lives today.
The same Christ who conquered death still saves sinners today.
The same grace that restored Peter still restores broken people today.
What lion-like warrior has God helped you overcome?
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
Sometimes it becomes part of someone else's salvation story.
The lion looked unstoppable until God entered the pit.
